description: Trillions of billions of planets, and yet radio silence. Science is looking for life elsewhere without promising little green men.

hero.hook: The universe is immense. So why is no one responding?

blocks.text: The observable universe contains approximately **2 trillion** galaxies, huge collections of stars, each with hundreds of billions of stars. With the help of statistics, the potentially habitable planets should be innumerable. Yet since the beginning of modern astronomy, we have had no confirmed contacts.

This contradiction has a name: the **Fermi** paradox, after the physicist **Enrico Fermi**. The question is no longer just science fiction. It comes under : the science which studies the conditions for the appearance of life elsewhere, and the means of detecting it. [[Exobiology]]

To look elsewhere, we start from the only known example: terrestrial life. It is mainly based on the chemistry of **carbon**, an atom which forms complex molecules, and on **liquid water**, which allows chemical reactions to take place well.

blocks.caption: Radio telescopes scan the sky, listening for a possible signal.

blocks.text: A candidate planet must often be in the [[habitable area]] of its star: neither too close, otherwise the water will evaporate, nor too far, otherwise the water will freeze. Since the 1990s, more than **5 500 exoplanets**, planets around stars other than the Sun, have been discovered. Almost every star in our galaxy would have at least one.
There are more stars in the observable universe than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth.

In **1961**, the astronomer **Frank Drake** proposed the [[Drake equation]]: a formula that multiplies factors — stars, habitable planets, duration of civilizations — to estimate the number of civilizations capable of communicating in the Milky Way. The figures remain very uncertain. The formula is mainly used to structure the debate.

No need to go to other stars right away. In our solar system, several worlds are intriguing. **Europe**, a moon of Jupiter, likely harbors an ocean of liquid water beneath a crust of ice. This ocean would remain liquid thanks to the [[Tidal forces]]: the enormous attraction of Jupiter deforms Europa and heats its interior by friction.

**Enceladus**, a small moon of Saturn, ejects **geysers**, jets of steam and matter. The **Cassini** probe found signs of **hydrothermal** activity there, heating by chemical reactions at the bottom of the ocean, capable in principle of feeding microbes without sunlight.

On **March**, liquid water once flowed on the surface. The robots are looking for : fossil or chemical traces of past life, before the planet lost a large part of its atmosphere and its water. [[Biosignatures]]

In **1950**, Fermi asks: If advanced civilizations exist in the thousands, why do we see no trace of them? The universe is old. A civilization only a million years ahead would have had time to stand out, even without traveling at the speed of light.

One hypothesis is that of : an almost impossible step to take in evolution, for example the transition to complex life, or technological self-destruction. Either we have already passed it, or it is in front of us. [[Large Filter]]

Other ideas: we may not be listening to the right signals. The **SETI** program, Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, mainly scans radio waves. Or the civilizations are too brief and too far away to cross paths. Or even the [[Zoo hypothesis]]: the Earth would be voluntarily left aside, like a reserve.

The **James Webb** space telescope analyzes light passing through the atmosphere of distant planets using , the cutting of light to identify the gases present. We look for gases like oxygen or methane in strange quantities, possible signs of life. [[Spectroscopy]]
If someone in the Andromeda Galaxy looked at us “right now”, they would see the Earth as it was **2.5 million years ago**: it takes this long for light to travel.

Even microbial life would change everything: it would prove that living things are not a unique accident. In the meantime, the **To travel** probes have been carrying golden discs with sounds and images of the Earth since **1977**. Probability of interception: almost zero. Need not to feel alone: ​​intact.
The planets are innumerable and life seems statistically plausible. But the absence of contact, the Fermi paradox, reminds us that technological intelligence could be very rare, or very brief.
